title: Ibrahim of Mosul and the Devil

keywords: ibrahim of mosul and the devil
full_text:
Ibrahim of Mosul, the chief court musician of the Abbasid empire, sat alone in his music salon in Baghdad, tuning his cedarwood lute. Having received the applause of emperors and scholars for thirty years, a subtle pride had taken root in his mind; he thought: 'Surely, in all the world, there is no melody I have not mastered, and no mode of rhythm that my fingers cannot execute with perfection.'

As the dusk gathered, an elderly traveler with a white beard, wearing a traveler’s woolen cloak and carrying a battered, plain wooden lute, stepped into the salon.

The stranger bowed respectfully: 'Peace be upon you, master of the lute. Will you permit an old wanderer to play a single melody upon his instrument in your presence?'

Ibrahim smiled with patronizing condescension: 'Play, old man; let us hear what simple country tunes you know.'

The old traveler sat cross-legged upon the carpet, tuned his plain wooden lute, and began to play.

The moment his fingers touched the gut strings, Ibrahim stood frozen in absolute awe! The music was unlike anything ever heard in the palaces of kings: it wept like the mountain wind through autumn cedars, whispered like running brook water over white pebbles, and soared like eagles into the sunset. The harmonies modulated across ancient, forgotten modes with effortless, divine perfection.

Ibrahim wept openly, his heart pierced with sublime joy and profound humility. He realized that compared to this master, his own celebrated art was merely the scraping of sticks.

When the melody concluded, the stranger stood, bowed with gentle dignity, and said: 'Remember, Ibrahim: art is as infinite as the heavens. He who thinks he has reached the summit has only blinded himself to the stars above.'

The mysterious master departed into the night, leaving Ibrahim to practice his lute with newfound humility and wonder for the rest of his days.
moral: True mastery in art recognizes that no musician knows all melodies; humility keeps the spirit open to learning.
